## Multiple Regression \(K=3\)
Multiple (or multivariate) regression is when we have more than one RHS variable (or covariate or regressor). Consider:

\begin{equation}
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + u.
\end{equation}

Assume we have a sample of data:
\[
\{(y_i, x_{1i}, x_{2i}) : i = 1, \dots, n\}.
\]

There are $K=3$ parameters to estimate. We need three exogeneity assumptions (moment conditions):

\begin{align}
E(u) &= 0 \quad \text{(A1)} \\
\text{Cov}(u, x_1) &= 0 \quad \text{(A2)} \\
\text{Cov}(u, x_2) &= 0 \quad \text{(A3)}
\end{align}

## Multiple Regression \(K\geq 3\)

The model extends to $K$ covariates:

\begin{equation}
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_K x_K + u.
\end{equation}

## When multiple regression fails
Multiple regression fails when:

\begin{enumerate}
\item Any regressor has no variation:
\[
\hat{Var(x_{ki})} = 0.
\]
\item There exists an exact linear combination between the \( x_{ki} \)s:
\[
\lambda_1 x_{1i} + \lambda_2 x_{2i} = \lambda_0.
\]
\end{enumerate}

This is known as \textbf{perfect multicollinearity}.

Examples:
\begin{align}
x_{1i} &= -\lambda_2 x_{2i} \quad (\lambda_1 = 1, \lambda_0 = 0) \\
x_{1i} + x_{2i} &= 1 \quad (\lambda_1 = \lambda_2 = \lambda_0 = 1)
\end{align}

## Firm-size and wages
\begin{itemize}
\item Larger firms pay higher wages than smaller firms.

\item In \texttt{20222 USoc extract.dta}, there is a variable which records
firm-size as one of K = 9 bands or bins or buckets::


$[1,2], [3,9], [10,24], [25,49], [50,99], [100,199], $
$[200,499], [500,999], [1000,\infty)$

\item \texttt{fsize} is actually an integer-valued ordered \textbf{multi-category
variable} that records the mid-point of each bin:

\[
1, 6, 17, 37, 75, 150, 350, 750, 1500.
\]

\end{itemize}

## Firm-size and wages: Model
\begin{itemize}
\item There are two strategies: (a) non-parametric (b) parametric.

\item For (a), we ``create'' $K = 9$ dummy variables:
\end{itemize}

\[
x_{1i} =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } 1 \le f_i^* \le 2 \\
0 & \text{else}
\end{cases}
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
x_{1i} = \mathbf{1}(1 \le f_i^* \le 2)
\]

\[
x_{2i} =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } 3 \le f_i^* \le 9 \\
0 & \text{else}
\end{cases}
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
x_{2i} = \mathbf{1}(3 \le f_i^* \le 9)
\]

\[
\vdots
\]
\vspace{-0.5cm}
\[
x_{9i} =
\begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } f_i^* \ge 1000 \\
0 & \text{else}
\end{cases}
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
x_{9i} = \mathbf{1}(f_i^* \ge 1000)
\]

\begin{itemize}
\item The $x_k$s are \texttt{fsize\_f1}, \texttt{fsize\_f6}, \ldots, \texttt{fsize\_f1500} in Ralf's pdf.

\item $f_k$ is \texttt{mfsize9} (recoded to \texttt{fsize}).
\end{itemize}

## Dummy Variable Trap

\begin{itemize}

\item The regression we wish run is written:
\[
\log y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{1i} + \beta_2 x_{2i}
+ \cdots + \beta_9 x_{9i} + u_i .
\]

\item \underline{However}, the computer cannot compute OLS estimates because
\[
x_{1i} + x_{2i} + \cdots + x_{9i} = 1
\quad \text{for every individual } i.
\]

This example of \textbf{perfect multi-collinearity} is also known as the
\textbf{dummy variable trap}.

\item We therefore drop a dummy, and actually choose the largest
firm-size category:
\begin{equation}
\log y = \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_8 x_8
+ \beta_0 + u. 
\end{equation}

\end{itemize}

## Interpreting the regression
\begin{itemize}

\item Repeating the $K=2$ case in Lecture 3, the $\beta$s are
interpreted as:
\[
\beta_1 \equiv 
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid x_1 = 1)
- 
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid x_9 = 1)
\]
\[
\vdots
\]
\[
\beta_8 \equiv 
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid x_8 = 1)
-
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid x_9 = 1)
\]

\[
\beta_0 \equiv 
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid x_9 = 1)
\]

\begin{itemize}
\item The $\beta$s can also be written:
\end{itemize}
\[
\beta_1 \equiv 
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid 1 \le f^* \le 2)
-
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid f^* \ge 1000)
\]
\[
\vdots
\]
\[
\beta_8 \equiv 
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid 500 \le f^* \le 999)
-
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid f^* \ge 1000)
\]
\[
\beta_0 \equiv 
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid f^* \ge 1000)
\]
\end{itemize}

## Interpreting the regression
\begin{itemize}
\item In words, $\beta_0$ is average log real hourly wage for the omitted or
base category (working for a firm employing 1000+ workers).
\item All the other $\beta_k$s are intepreted as the population raw diﬀerential
in log real hourly wages between the firm-size category that $\beta_k$ “belongs to” and the largest firm-size category.
\item These are estimated by the corresponding raw diﬀerentials and are
measured in log-points.
\end{itemize}


## Estimating the regression
\begin{itemize}

\item The results are in Ralf's \texttt{Regression\_Multiple.html}.

\item See the \underline{second} regression for the estimation of (8).

\item The parameters are interpreted as above. The estimate on the
constant is $2.615$ $(0.007)$ and is average log-pay for those working
in the largest firm-size category (1000+).

\item The estimate on \texttt{fsize\_f1} is $-0.548$ and is the raw differential
in log real hourly wage between those in the smallest firm-size
category (1--2) and those in the largest firm-size category (1000+).
It is large, and converts to a differential of about $-42.2\%$.

\item In both cases, exactly the same estimates can be calculated from
the \texttt{tibble}.

\end{itemize}


## Do we really have 59k data points?
\begin{itemize}

\item Just as there were 2 population means when we have a gender
dummy, here we have:
\[
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid k = j), 
\qquad j = 1, \ldots, 9.
\]

\item This means there are just 9 fitted values, depending on which
firm-size category the individual belongs to.

\item But there are 58,789 individual-years (datapoints).

\item So one can think of regression as ``collapsing'' the data to just 9
data-points:
\[
\left\{ \left( \overline{\log y_k},\, f_k \right) : 
k = 1, \ldots, 9 \right\}.
\]

\item See the earlier \texttt{tibble}. All the regression does is
replicate this information.

\item So what is the benefit of having micro-econometric data?
Each cell-mean $\overline{\log y_k}$ is estimated from $n_k$ obs.
Without knowing $n_k$, inference is not possible.

\end{itemize}

## Modelling the 9 datapoints

\begin{itemize}

\item In the next 4 slides, we model these 9 datapoints.

\item These are the red blobs. They seem to follow some non-linear
relationship.

\item What is the blue line? It is the second \textbf{parametric}
strategy we could adopt for modelling this relationship.
Here we choose a log--log model:
\[
\log y = \delta_0 + \delta_1 \log f + \text{error}.
\]

\end{itemize}

## Alternative parametric models

\begin{itemize}

\item One can see that log--log relationship is a reasonable fit.
The estimate of $\hat{\delta}_1$ is $0.0896$ $(0.0014)$.
It is an elasticity (unit-free).

\item Other \textbf{parametric} models could be fitted, eg a quadratic:
\[
\log y = \delta_0 + \delta_1 f + \delta_2 f^2 + \text{error}.
\]

The relationship between log-pay and age is often modelled like this.

\end{itemize}


## Conclusion
\begin{itemize}
\item Multiple regression is the basic tool in econometrics.
\item We have illustrated its use in just one example.
\item Many more examples will appear later.
\item It seems to be the case that large firms pay more than smaller
firms. But only the raw data have been used.
\item So we cannot interpret this relationship as causal. We could and
should add more covariates, like age and education, but . . .
\item OLS cannot deal the fact that individuals choose where to work,
and know that larger firms pay more than smaller ones, ceteris
paribus. Similarly, good firms will choose to hire workers with high innate ability (unobserved)
and pay them more. 
\end{itemize}


## Controlling for observables
\begin{itemize}

\item The basic idea is that we add as many relevant variables as we can
to a model, to mitigate/minimise \underline{some} of the effect of omitted
variables bias (OVB). Recall Lecture 4.

\item But there is often something fundamentally unobserved.

\item In
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + \cdots + \beta_K x_K + u
\]
\[
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \mathbf{x}'\mathbf{b} + u
\]

$\beta_1$ is the effect of interest. All the other variables are
\textbf{controls}.

\item Notation:
\[
\mathbf{x}' = (x_2, \ldots, x_K)
\qquad
\mathbf{b}' = (\beta_2, \ldots, \beta_K).
\]

\item Often $x_1$ is a dummy $d$.

\item A concrete example is at the end of this topic.

\end{itemize}

## Long and short regressions
\begin{itemize}

\item When estimating
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 d + \mathbf{x}'\mathbf{b} + u
\]
the conditional differential is
\[
\mathbb{E}(y \mid \mathbf{x}', d = 1)
-
\mathbb{E}(y \mid \mathbf{x}', d = 0).
\]

\item When estimating
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 d + u
\]
the unconditional differential is
\[
\mathbb{E}(y \mid d = 1)
-
\mathbb{E}(y \mid d = 0).
\]

\item But do the OLS estimates differ from each other?
Define $\widehat{\beta}_1$ as the OLS estimate from the long regression
and $\widetilde{\beta}_1$ as the OLS estimate from the short regression.

\item When the long contains one extra regressor we already know what
happens (almost) \ldots

\end{itemize}

## OVB again
\begin{itemize}

\item Compare the estimates from:
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2 + e 
\qquad \text{(L)}
\]
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + u,
\qquad \text{(S)}
\]

with $\mathrm{Cov}(e, x_1) = \mathrm{Cov}(e, x_2) = \mathbb{E}(e) = 0$.

\item When estimating (S), the OVB formula from Lecture 4 says:
\[
\mathrm{Bias}(\widetilde{\beta}_1)
\equiv
\mathbb{E}(\widetilde{\beta}_1) - \beta_1
=
\beta_2
\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x_2, x_1)}{\mathrm{Var}(x_1)}
=
\beta_2 \delta_1,
\]

where $\delta_1$ is the ``slope'' parameter:
\[
x_2 = \delta_0 + \delta_1 x_1 + \text{error}.
\]

\item When estimating (L), the OVB formula says the bias is zero:
\[
\mathrm{Bias}(\widehat{\beta}_1)
\equiv
\mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1) - \beta_1
=
0.
\]

\end{itemize}

## OVB again
\begin{itemize}

\item \[
\mathbb{E}(\widetilde{\beta}_1) - \mathbb{E}(\widehat{\beta}_1)
= \beta_2 \delta_1.
\]

\item It turns out that this holds \underline{exactly} in the data:
\[
\widetilde{\beta}_1 - \widehat{\beta}_1
=
\widehat{\beta}_2 \widehat{\delta}_1.
\]

\item When the long regression is longer than 2 covariates
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \beta_2 x_2
+ \cdots + \beta_K x_K + e,
\qquad \text{(L$'$)}
\]

the formula does not hold exactly, but it still works in principle.

\item This formula is very, very useful.

\end{itemize}

## Lifetime earnings and a university degree

\begin{itemize}

\item Consider the model:
\[
y = \beta_0 + \tau d + \beta_1 a + \beta_2 a^2
+ \mathbf{x}'\mathbf{b} + u
\]

where $y$ is earnings, $d$ is a graduate dummy, and $a$ is age.

\item If we assume all the RHS variables are exogenous:
\[
\mathbb{E}(y \mid a, \mathbf{x}', d = 1)
=
\beta_0 + \tau + \beta_1 a + \beta_2 a^2
+ \mathbf{x}'\mathbf{b}
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}(y \mid a, \mathbf{x}', d = 0)
=
\beta_0 + \beta_1 a + \beta_2 a^2
+ \mathbf{x}'\mathbf{b}
\]

and so
\[
\tau
=
\mathbb{E}(y \mid a, \mathbf{x}', d = 1)
-
\mathbb{E}(y \mid a, \mathbf{x}', d = 0)
\]

is the so-called \textbf{conditional differential}
(or \textbf{conditional treatment effect} if appropriate).

\item Conceptually different from the \textbf{unconditional differential}
\[
\mathbb{E}(y \mid d = 1)
-
\mathbb{E}(y \mid d = 0).
\]

\end{itemize}

## Two parallel CEFs
\begin{itemize}

\item Because everything comes from the same regression, everything
nets out, especially age $a$.

\item In other words, the 2 so-called \textbf{Conditional Expectation
Functions} (CEFs) are parallel when plotted in the same picture.

\item Plotting them can be pain because of the term $\mathbf{x}'\mathbf{b}$,
after its been estimated:
\[
\mathbf{x}'\widehat{\mathbf{b}}
=
\widehat{\beta}_2 \,\overline{x}_2
+ \cdots +
\widehat{\beta}_K \,\overline{x}_K
\]

But it only affects the constant.

\item The next slide shows what happens in the BHPS/US.

\item But is the slide after more realistic?

\end{itemize}

## Two non-parallel CEFs
\begin{itemize}

\item How do we make the age-relationship vary by $d$?
Add 2 interaction terms:
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 a + \beta_2 a^2
+ \tau_0 d + \tau_1 da + \tau_2 da^2
+ \mathbf{x}'\mathbf{b} + u.
\]

\item Rewriting the CEFs:
\[
\mathbb{E}(y \mid a, \mathbf{x}', d = 1)
=
\beta_0 + \beta_1 a + \beta_2 a^2
+ \tau_0 + \tau_1 a + \tau_2 a^2
+ \mathbf{x}'\mathbf{b}
\]
\[
\mathbb{E}(y \mid a, \mathbf{x}', d = 0)
=
\beta_0 + \beta_1 a + \beta_2 a^2
+ \mathbf{x}'\mathbf{b}
\]

and so
\[
\mathbb{E}(y \mid a, \mathbf{x}', d = 1)
-
\mathbb{E}(y \mid a, \mathbf{x}', d = 0)
=
\tau_0 + \tau_1 a + \tau_2 a^2.
\]

\item This can be computed at any age.
The IFS do this at $a = 29$.

\item For a Lifetime Earnings measure:
\[
\int_{a=18}^{65}
(\tau_0 + \tau_1 a + \tau_2 a^2)\, da
=
\left[
\tau_0 a
+ \frac{\tau_1}{2} a^2
+ \frac{\tau_2}{3} a^3
\right]_{18}^{65}.
\]

\end{itemize}

## Walker and Zhu

\begin{itemize}
\item "Differences by degree: Evidence of the net financial rates of
return to undergraduate study for England and Wales"
\item WZ extend the framework as follows.
First write our non-parallel models as:
\[
\log y
=
(\beta_0 + \tau_0)
+
(\beta_1 + \tau_1)a
+
(\beta_2 + \tau_2)a^2
+
\mathbf{x}'\mathbf{b}
+
u
\qquad \text{if } d = 1
\]

\[
\log y
=
\beta_0 + \beta_1 a + \beta_2 a^2
+
\mathbf{x}'\mathbf{b}
+
u
\qquad \text{if } d = 0
\]
\item Instead of 2 categories, we could have $Q$:
\[
\log y_q
=
\beta_0^q
+
\beta_1^q a_q
+
\beta_2^q a_q^2
+
\sum_j \lambda^{jq} D_q^j
+
\mathbf{x}_q'\mathbf{b}^q
+
u_q,
\qquad q = 1, \ldots, Q
\]
\item Instead of looking at graduate ($d=1$) and else ($d=0$),
WZ condition on those eligible to go to university and split these by $q$:
\begin{itemize}
\item STEM, LEM, COMB, OSSAH; first class, upper second, below upper second, degree class missing.
\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}

## Walker and Zhu
\begin{itemize}

\item This is WZ's Equation (2), except ours is a population model
whereas there's is a sample model (data are indexed by $i$).

\item The $D^j$'s are dummies for `qualification' category/level:
doctoral, master, PGCE, \ldots, first degree, 2+ A-levels.

\item Hence the $\lambda^{jq}$'s are:
\[
\lambda^{jq}
=
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid \mathbf{x}', \text{qual} = j)
-
\mathbb{E}(\log y \mid \mathbf{x}', \text{qual} = 0)
\qquad
\text{for } q = 1, \ldots, Q
\]

\item WZ use the Labour Force Survey (LFS), whereas the above is from
BHPS/US. Why?: much better info on degree.

\item The LFS is a rolling panel (each $i$ observed 5 quarters then exit).
BHPS/US is `proper' panel.

\item WZ split by gender throughout (absolutely standard) whereas my
results above are for males.

\end{itemize}

## Walker and Zhu
\begin{itemize}
\item WZ model the real hourly wage rate, logged, whereas I model
real annual pay, unlogged. WZ also worry about lifetime earnings,
NPVs, IRRs.
\item WZ write down their model in terms of years of labour market
experience (the latent variable) but proxy it by age.
This raises issues relating to measurement error biases.
I model age from the outset.
\item There are lots of tables of descriptives (xtabs), figures,
and regressions. This is because their analysis is multi-dimensional,
relating to:
\begin{itemize}
\item educational attainment/level
\item degree classification
\item degree subject
\item gender
\item age/experience
\end{itemize}

\end{itemize}
